title: Hitler's Germany: emergence, consolidation and rule
summary: How Hitler rose to power through the crises of Weimar, consolidated a dictatorship in 1933–34, and ruled through terror, propaganda and a racial state.

keyterms.definition: Failed Nazi attempt to seize power in Bavaria in November 1923; Hitler was jailed and wrote Mein Kampf.
Weimar constitutional clause letting the president rule by emergency decree, used heavily from 1930.
March 1933 law letting Hitler's cabinet pass laws without the Reichstag for four years.
February 1933 emergency decree suspending civil liberties after the Reichstag fire, used to arrest communists.
'Coordination': bringing all institutions, from state governments to trade unions and clubs, under Nazi control.
30 June 1934 purge of SA leader Ernst Röhm and other rivals, which secured army support for Hitler.
1935 laws stripping German Jews of citizenship and banning marriage between Jews and non-Jews.
Pogrom of 9–10 November 1938 in which synagogues, Jewish homes and businesses were attacked and about 30,000 Jewish men arrested.
Ian Kershaw's idea that officials radicalised policy by anticipating what Hitler wanted, rather than following detailed orders.
1936 economic programme under Göring to make Germany ready for war and self-sufficient (autarky).

questions.prompt: What was the most important lesson Hitler drew from the failed Munich Putsch?
options: Power should be won through elections and legal means
Germany needed an alliance with the USSR
The army would always support him
questions.explanation: After 1923 Hitler pursued a 'legality' strategy, while still using SA violence on the streets.

questions.text: In the July 1932 election the Nazis won about ___% of the vote, becoming the largest party.
questions.explanation: They won 230 seats but never gained a majority in a free election; their vote fell to about 33% in November 1932.

questions.statement: Hitler became chancellor by winning a majority in the Reichstag.
questions.explanation: President Hindenburg appointed him on 30 January 1933 after backroom deals led by Franz von Papen, who believed Hitler could be controlled.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in Hitler's consolidation of power in order.
items: Hitler becomes Führer on Hindenburg's death
questions.explanation: January, February, March and May 1933; June 1934; August 1934.

questions.prompt: Why was the Enabling Act so important?
options: It gave the cabinet power to make laws without the Reichstag
questions.explanation: Passed with Centre Party votes while communists were excluded, it provided a legal basis for dictatorship.

questions.prompt: Match each factor to its role in Hitler's rise.

pairs.right: Mass unemployment boosted the Nazi vote

questions.explanation: Historians weigh economic crisis, political intrigue and Nazi appeal when explaining 1933.

questions.text: Bringing all organisations under Nazi control was called ___.
questions.explanation: State parliaments, trade unions and other parties were absorbed or abolished in 1933.

questions.prompt: Why did Hitler purge the SA in June 1934?
options: To win the army's support and remove Röhm's threat of a 'second revolution'
Because the SA had joined the communists
To please the League of Nations
questions.explanation: The army leadership feared the SA; after the purge it swore a personal oath to Hitler in August 1934.

questions.statement: The Reichstag Fire Decree suspended civil liberties such as freedom of speech and assembly.
questions.explanation: It allowed mass arrests of communists before the March 1933 election.

questions.prompt: Which group gave the Nazis a disproportionately strong share of their vote by 1932?
options: Catholic industrial workers in the Ruhr
questions.explanation: Electoral studies show strong Nazi support in Protestant, rural and middle-class areas; Catholic and working-class areas were more resistant.

questions.prompt: Who led the SS and later the whole police apparatus?
questions.explanation: Himmler became chief of German police in 1936, combining the SS and Gestapo into a vast terror system.

questions.text: The 1935 ___ Laws removed German citizenship from Jews.
questions.explanation: They also banned marriages and sexual relations between Jews and 'Aryans'.

questions.prompt: Put these stages of anti-Jewish persecution in order.
questions.explanation: April 1933, September 1935, November 1938, January 1942: persecution radicalised in stages.

questions.statement: Recent research suggests the Gestapo relied heavily on denunciations from ordinary Germans.
questions.explanation: Historians such as Robert Gellately showed the Gestapo was small and depended on public informers, revealing a degree of consent.

questions.prompt: What was the main aim of Göring's Four-Year Plan (1936)?
options: Prepare the economy for war and autarky
Reduce the size of the army
questions.explanation: It prioritised rearmament and synthetic substitutes for imports, at the expense of consumer goods ('guns before butter').

questions.prompt: Match each organisation to its function.

pairs.right: Controlled artists, writers and the press

questions.explanation: Such organisations aimed to build a Volksgemeinschaft (people's community) loyal to the regime.

questions.prompt: What agreement did Hitler make with the Catholic Church in July 1933?
options: The Concordat, guaranteeing Church rights if clergy stayed out of politics
questions.explanation: The regime soon broke the Concordat; Pope Pius XI criticised Nazism in the 1937 encyclical 'With Burning Concern'.

questions.text: Ian Kershaw described officials anticipating Hitler's wishes as 'working towards the ___'.
questions.explanation: This idea bridges intentionalist and structuralist interpretations of how the regime worked.

questions.statement: Structuralist historians such as Hans Mommsen argued that Hitler was in some respects a 'weak dictator'.
questions.explanation: They stressed chaotic, competing agencies that drove 'cumulative radicalisation', while intentionalists stress Hitler's ideology and plans.

questions.prompt: Which economic achievement most helped the regime's popularity?
options: Rapid fall in unemployment through public works and rearmament
Rising real wages far above 1928 levels
questions.explanation: Registered unemployment fell from about 6 million in early 1933 to near zero by 1938, though real wages stayed low and women and Jews were removed from statistics.
